A combinatorial threshold-linear network (CTLN) is a threshold-linear network fully specified by a simple directed graph GG on nn nodes and three positive parameters ε,δ,θε,δ,θ (Section 2.3). With uniform input θθ, activity obeys equation (1): dxidt=−xi+[∑j=1nWijxj+θ]+,[y]+=max⁡{y,0},dtdxi​​=−xi​+[j=1∑n​Wij​xj​+θ]+​,[y]+​=max{y,0}, with weights from equation (3): Wij={0if i=j,−1+εif j→i in G,−1−δotherwise,0<ε<1, δ>0.Wij​=⎩⎨⎧​0−1+ε−1−δ​if i=j,if j→i in G,otherwise,​0<ε<1, δ>0. Here WijWij​ is the effect of node jj on node ii.

Every interaction is inhibitory, so the network is competitive (Wij≤0Wij​≤0, Wii=0Wii​=0, nonnegative inputs). An edge j→ij→i gives Wij>−1Wij​>−1, so jj inhibits ii less than the normalised self-inhibition, −1−1 (weak inhibition). A missing edge gives Wij<−1Wij​<−1 (strong inhibition). The paper interprets GG as connections among excitatory neurons amid strong background inhibition (Figure 1A). Weak inhibition is an excitatory connection added to that background, so an edge is still net inhibitory, not literal excitation.

The parameters are usually kept in the legal range ε<δ/(δ+1)ε<δ/(δ+1) (Definition 2.3). In this range, two nodes joined by a one-way edge cannot be the support (set of active nodes) of a stable fixed point: their block (−I+W){i,j}(−I+W){i,j}​ has trace −2−2 and determinant ε(1+δ)−δ<0ε(1+δ)−δ<0. Theorem 3.4 also assumes it: if GG is oriented (no bidirectional edges) and has no sinks (every node has an outgoing edge), then a nondegenerate CTLN (certain determinants are nonzero; Definition 5.1) has bounded activity and no stable fixed points.

Take the 3-cycle 1→2→3→11→2→3→1 (Figure 1C) with only node 1 active, at x1=θx1​=θ. Node 2 receives θ+(−1+ε)θ=εθ>0θ+(−1+ε)θ=εθ>0 and rises. Node 3 receives −δθ<0−δθ<0 and stays silent. The paper describes this as promoting the flow of activity along the arrows (Section 2.3).

The paper gives conditions under which a competitive threshold-linear network has bounded activity and no stable fixed points. Earlier theory focused on stable fixed points of symmetric networks, as in Hopfield-type memories. Rhythms and sequences are more naturally modeled by dynamic attractors (Sections 1 and 3.2).

A threshold-linear network (TLN) on nn nodes satisfies dxidt=−xi+[∑j=1nWijxj+bi]+,[y]+=max⁡{y,0},dtdxi​​=−xi​+[j=1∑n​Wij​xj​+bi​]+​,[y]+​=max{y,0}, where WijWij​ is the effect of node jj on node ii and bibi​ is the external drive. The theorems assume competitiveness (Wij≤0Wij​≤0, Wii=0Wii​=0, bi≥0bi​≥0), which bounds activity (Lemma 2.1), and nondegeneracy (certain determinants are nonzero and some bi>0bi​>0, Definition 5.1). A fixed point’s support σσ is its set of active nodes.

  • Parity (Theorem 3.1). If every bi>0bi​>0, the fixed-point indices idx⁡(σ)=sgn⁡det⁡(I−Wσ)idx(σ)=sgndet(I−Wσ​) sum to +1+1, where WσWσ​ is the principal submatrix on σσ. Thus the number of fixed points is odd. Stable fixed points have index +1+1, so at most 2n−12n−1 fixed points are stable (Corollary 3.2).
  • No stable steady states (Theorem 3.3). For uniform inputs bi=θbi​=θ, draw an edge j→ij→i (i≠ji=j) whenever Wij>−1Wij​>−1. If the graph is oriented (no bidirectional edges), has no sinks (every node has an outgoing edge), and Wij<1/WjiWij​<1/Wji​ on every edge j→ij→i, fixed points exist by Theorem 3.1 and all are unstable.
  • CTLNs (Theorem 3.4). A combinatorial TLN (CTLN) on a simple directed graph GG has bi=θ>0bi​=θ>0 and Wii=0Wii​=0. Off-diagonal weights are Wij=−1+εWij​=−1+ε for edges j→ij→i (weak inhibition) and Wij=−1−δWij​=−1−δ otherwise, with 0<ε<10<ε<1 and δ>0δ>0. In the legal range ε<δ/(δ+1)ε<δ/(δ+1), one-way edges automatically satisfy the weight condition. A nondegenerate CTLN in this range on an oriented graph without sinks therefore has bounded activity and no stable fixed points.
  • Cliques (Theorem 3.5). For a nondegenerate CTLN on any simple directed graph with ε,δ,θ>0ε,δ,θ>0 and ε<1ε<1, even beyond the legal range, a clique (pairwise bidirectionally connected nodes) supports a stable fixed point exactly when it is target-free (no outside node receives edges from every member). The theorem leaves nonclique supports unclassified.

Conjecture 3.6 proposed that in the legal range only target-free cliques support stable fixed points. Jesse Geneson disproved it (2026, arXiv:2607.21396) with a legal, nondegenerate six-neuron CTLN whose stable fixed point activates all six neurons although two share no edge.

Section 4 identifies dynamic attractors numerically. At ε=0.25ε=0.25, δ=0.5δ=0.5, θ=1θ=1, three oriented 25-node graphs without sinks exhibit a limit cycle, a chaotic attractor and quasi-periodic behaviour (Figure 2). In one 9-node network, the initial condition alone selects among two stable fixed points, a limit cycle and a chaotic attractor (Figure 4). Using cliques with targets, which cannot support stable fixed points by Theorem 3.5, the paper designs a quadruped central pattern generator (a rhythm-generating circuit) whose initial condition selects a bound or trot gait (Figure 10).

In simulations, combinatorial threshold-linear networks (CTLNs) show stable fixed points, limit cycles, quasi-periodic attractors and chaos. Several attractors, even of different types, can coexist in one network. The initial condition alone then selects which one is reached (Section 4.1). Other observed behaviours include limit cycles with irregular emergent sequences (Figure 5) or quasi-synchronous rhythms (Figure 8), the apparently novel "Gaudi attractor" (Figure 6), a spontaneous switch from irregular to periodic activity (Figure 9), and engineered networks with coexisting quadruped-gait limit cycles (Figure 10).

A CTLN on a directed graph GG has dynamics dxidt=−xi+[∑jWijxj+θ]+,[y]+=max⁡{y,0},dtdxi​​=−xi​+[j∑​Wij​xj​+θ]+​,[y]+​=max{y,0}, with weights Wij={0if i=j,−1+εif j→i in G(weak inhibition),−1−δotherwise(strong inhibition).Wij​=⎩⎨⎧​0−1+ε−1−δ​if i=j,if j→i in G(weak inhibition),otherwise(strong inhibition).​ The simulations use the standard parameters ε=0.25ε=0.25, δ=0.5δ=0.5, θ=1θ=1 unless a figure says otherwise. When the parameters are the same, differences between networks come only from GG.

Figure 2 shows three CTLNs on 25-node graphs. The top row gives their adjacency matrices, and the bottom row gives random two-dimensional projections of their trajectories. The networks produce a limit cycle (A), a chaotic attractor (B) and quasi-periodic behaviour (C). The quasi-periodic case comes from a highly structured graph. Each graph is oriented (no bidirectional edges) and has no sinks (every node has an outgoing edge). Theorem 3.4 therefore guarantees bounded activity and no stable fixed points, provided the CTLN is nondegenerate (certain determinants are nonzero, Definition 5.1) and its parameters are in the legal range ε<δ/(δ+1)ε<δ/(δ+1).

Which dynamic attractor actually appears is a numerical finding that the theorems do not predict.

To design a gait, connect the nodes for legs that should fire together in both directions, then give each pair a common downstream target. Figure 10 uses this idea to build a single central pattern generator in which the initial activity selects either a bound or a trot.

In a combinatorial threshold-linear network (CTLN), the firing rate xixi​ obeys x˙i=−xi+[∑jWijxj+θ]+x˙i​=−xi​+[∑j​Wij​xj​+θ]+​, with [y]+=max⁡{y,0}[y]+​=max{y,0} and uniform drive θ>0θ>0. The network is competitive. It has Wii=0Wii​=0, and an edge j→ij→i gives weaker inhibition from jj to ii (Wij=−1+εWij​=−1+ε) than an absent edge (Wij=−1−δWij​=−1−δ), with 0<ε<10<ε<1 and δ>0δ>0 (Section 2.3). Both theorems below assume nondegeneracy, meaning the fixed-point determinants specified in Definition 5.1 are nonzero.

Theorem 3.5 gives the rule used for the leg pairs. A clique is a group connected pairwise in both directions. It supports a stable fixed point with exactly its members active if and only if it is target-free. A target is an outside node that receives an edge from every clique member. At the clique’s candidate equilibrium, the target receives positive net input, so it cannot remain silent (Section 5.6). Hence a leg pair with a target cannot be the support of a stable fixed point. Section 4.4 observes that activity instead flows on to the target and then to the next pair. The theorem says nothing about stable fixed points whose supports are not cliques.

For the bound, arrange four groups in cyclic order: the front-leg pair, an auxiliary node, the hind-leg pair, and a second auxiliary node. The only edges between groups run from every node in one group to every node in the next, including the return to the front pair. Each pair is a clique with the following auxiliary node as its target. In the simulated rhythm, the front legs fire together and alternate with the hind legs. For the trot, use the same construction with diagonal leg pairs (Figure 10A).

To combine the gaits, merge the four corresponding leg nodes, retain all edges, and keep the four auxiliary nodes distinct. Simulations of this eight-node network show two coexisting limit cycles at the same weights and drive (Figure 10B). Section 4.5 notes that the mathematical properties of this gluing are not well understood. Even so, simulations show that it often preserves the component rhythms.

Theorem 3.4 offers a separate design rule. In the legal range 0<ε<δ/(1+δ)0<ε<δ/(1+δ), an oriented graph (no bidirectional edges) with no sinks (every node has an outgoing edge) guarantees bounded activity and excludes stable fixed points. The gait circuits fall outside this rule because their leg pairs have reciprocal edges. Their particular firing sequences are simulation results.

Yes: it was disproved. Jesse Geneson (2026) gave a six-neuron combinatorial threshold-linear network (CTLN) with a stable fixed point at which all six neurons are active, even though neurons 4 and 5 have no edge in either direction. Geneson's Theorem 3.2 proves that the same graph gives a nondegenerate counterexample for every uniform drive θ>0θ>0 and all sufficiently small ε>0ε>0 with δ=29ε/25δ=29ε/25. These parameters satisfy the strict legal bound 0<ε<δ/(1+δ)0<ε<δ/(1+δ) of Definition 2.3. arXiv:2607.21396

Conjecture 3.6 is stated in Section 3.3, right after Theorem 3.5. It concerns a nondegenerate CTLN (Definition 5.1: certain determinants are nonzero) on a simple directed graph GG, with weights Wii=0Wii​=0 and, for i≠ji=j, Wij=−1+εWij​=−1+ε if j→ij→i and −1−δ−1−δ otherwise, and with ε,δε,δ in the legal range. It asserts that a stable fixed point with support σσ (the set of neurons with positive activity) exists if and only if σσ is a target-free clique. This means that every pair in σσ is connected in both directions and that no vertex outside σσ receives an edge from every member. The paper reported that it had found no counterexample. In Geneson's example, the support contains every vertex, so it has no outside target. The clique condition fails, however, for the pair 4, 5.

The paper's Theorem 3.5 still gives an exact test for a set that is a clique: it supports a stable fixed point precisely when it is target-free. This holds for any nondegenerate CTLN on a simple directed graph with θ,δ>0θ,δ>0 and 0<ε<10<ε<1, even beyond the legal range. Morrison, Degeratu, Itskov and Curto (2024)

The full classification has also been proved in special cases. For symmetric graphs, the target-free cliques are exactly the maximal cliques, and these are exactly the stable supports (Curto and Morrison (2016)). Within the legal range, the classification holds for supports of at most four neurons in a network of any size. It also holds for every graph on nn vertices when δ(1−ε)/ε>n2−n−1δ(1−ε)/ε>n2−n−1 (Curto, Geneson and Morrison (2024)). Geneson's Theorem 4.1 proves it for every nondegenerate legal CTLN on n≥3n≥3 vertices whenever δ(1−ε)/ε≥n−2−(n−3)ε/2δ(1−ε)/ε≥n−2−(n−3)ε/2.
